title: The Environment and Economics in the Global Age
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: Beginning in 1958, scientist Charles Keeling measured carbon dioxide in the atmosphere at a Hawaiian observatory and recorded a steadily rising trend. The resulting Keeling Curve was the first clear, continuous evidence that human activity was changing the chemistry of the entire planet's atmosphere.

The same global economy that generated unprecedented wealth, lifted billions out of poverty, and connected the world after 1900 also placed unprecedented strain on the natural environment, to the point of altering the climate of the whole planet.

The world's population surged from roughly 1.6 billion in 1900 to past 6 billion by 2000 and toward 8 billion afterward, the fastest growth in human history, made possible by industrial food production, modern medicine, and sanitation.

Alongside population growth, average consumption of energy, goods, and resources soared, especially in the wealthy industrialized world. More people each consuming far more placed enormous and growing pressure on the planet's land, water, forests, and atmosphere.

Modern economic growth caused widespread environmental damage: deforestation cleared vast areas, especially tropical rainforests; pollution of air, water, and soil spread with industry and cities; fresh water, fisheries, and biodiversity came under severe strain; and species extinction accelerated dramatically.

Climate change (global warming) is driven mainly by the burning of fossil fuels — coal, oil, and natural gas — the energy foundation of industrial civilization. This releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, gradually warming the planet.

The effects of climate change include rising temperatures and sea levels, melting ice, more extreme weather, and disruptions to agriculture and ecosystems, making it the defining global environmental challenge of the contemporary era.

Climate change reveals a deep injustice: the wealthy industrialized nations produced the great majority of historical greenhouse emissions, yet many of the worst consequences fall on poorer nations least able to cope and least responsible for the problem.

After 1945, and especially after the Cold War ended around 1991, the dominant trend was toward integration and the worldwide spread of free-market capitalism, replacing the Cold War's divided capitalist and communist economic order with a single global economy.

Free trade — the reduction of tariffs and barriers to the movement of goods and money across borders — expanded dramatically, on the theory that open markets make everyone richer, and became a central feature of the globalized economy.

Multinational corporations (MNCs) are huge companies operating across many countries, some richer than entire nations. They became central players in the global economy, building global supply chains and shifting production to wherever labor and costs were most favorable.

The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), established after World War II, lent money and shaped economic policy in developing nations, becoming influential and sometimes controversial institutions of the global economy.

The World Trade Organization (WTO), founded in 1995, worked to lower trade barriers and set the rules of global commerce, while regional blocs like the European Union and agreements like NAFTA further knit economies together.

After Mao's death, China under Deng Xiaoping began from 1978 to open its economy to markets, foreign investment, and trade while keeping Communist Party political control. This turned China into the world's manufacturing powerhouse and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty.

By the early twenty-first century, nearly the entire world participated in a single capitalist global economy, including formerly communist states after the collapse of the USSR — a dramatic change from the divided economic world of the Cold War.

Supporters argue economic globalization provides jobs, investment, technology, and skills, gives consumers cheaper goods, and has lifted hundreds of millions — especially in China and East Asia — out of extreme poverty, arguably the greatest poverty reduction in human history.

Critics argue economic globalization can impose sweatshop wages and harsh conditions, exploit weak labor and environmental laws, give multinational corporations more power than governments, devastate communities when factories relocate, and distribute benefits with stark inequality.

Economic globalization both reduced absolute poverty for hundreds of millions and increased certain inequalities: global wealth soared, but so did the gap between the richest and the rest, both between nations and within them. Its effects were uneven, helping some regions and groups while hurting others.

Evaluating a historical debate requires defining the question clearly, presenting the strongest evidence for each side, taking a defensible and often nuanced position, and acknowledging counter-arguments and complexity rather than simply praising or condemning.

The most valuable analytical frame for globalization is that its effects were double-edged and unevenly distributed: it reduced poverty AND widened inequality, brought prosperity AND climate change, with winners and losers in every dimension.

Climate change poses a challenge unlike any in prior history: a threat to the entire species that no nation can solve alone, demanding global cooperation that the fragmented, competitive world of nation-states finds difficult to achieve.

The global economy and its environmental consequences are the culmination of trends running through the whole course: the environmental crisis extends the fossil-fuel industrialization of the 1800s, and the global economy's core-periphery patterns extend the economic relationships of imperialism into the present.
